title: Spiking Neural Networks: The Future of Brain-Inspired Computing
venue: International Journal of Engineering Trends and Technology
tldr: Compares surrogate gradient, ANN-to-SNN conversion, and STDP-based Spiking Neural Networks across accuracy, latency, energy, spike count, and convergence under a unified protocol.
problem_and_motivation: No single existing study compares all major SNN training paradigms under a unified protocol across multiple performance dimensions. This gap obscures practical tradeoffs for edge deployment and real-time robotics, where accuracy, latency, energy, and convergence must be balanced simultaneously.
approach: Evaluates three SNN training paradigms: surrogate gradient descent, ANN-to-SNN conversion, and STDP under a unified experimental protocol.
Uses MNIST, CIFAR-10, DVS128 Gesture, SHD, and SSC datasets as benchmarks for static and event-based tasks.
Simulates surrogate gradient SNNs in Brian2, ANN-to-SNN conversion in BindsNET, and large-scale STDP models in NEST.
Measures five metrics: classification accuracy, inference latency, energy per inference, spike count, and convergence rate over 20 epochs.
Runs each experiment five times with varying random seeds and reports mean plus standard deviation.
findings: num: Surrogate gradient SNNs achieve 97.8% on MNIST and 85.7% on CIFAR-10, within 1-2% of ANN baselines.
num: Converted SNNs reach 98.1% on MNIST and 89.3% on CIFAR-10 with 90% energy reduction.
num: STDP-based SNNs consume as low as 5 mJ per inference with 95.5% MNIST accuracy.
num: Surrogate gradient SNNs converge fastest, reducing loss from 0.9 to 0.44 by epoch 20.
num: Inference latency of surrogate gradient SNNs is approximately 10 ms, compared to 45 ms for ANNs.
num: SNNs achieve 90-97% energy savings relative to ANNs with only 1-3% accuracy drop.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper provides a unified, multi-dimensional comparison of three major SNN training paradigms under a single experimental protocol, which was previously absent in the literature. It reports accuracy, latency, energy per inference, spike count, and convergence simultaneously, enabling principled model selection for neuromorphic computing. The study demonstrates that surrogate gradient SNNs achieve near-ANN accuracy with significantly lower energy and latency, while STDP-based models offer maximal energy efficiency at a moderate accuracy cost. It also quantifies the tradeoffs between training paradigms across static and event-based datasets, providing actionable guidance for deployment-oriented SNN design.
directly_justifies: Surrogate gradient SNNs achieve within 1-2% of ANN accuracy with faster convergence by epoch 20.
STDP-based SNNs consume as low as 5 mJ per inference with highly sparse spiking activity.
Converted SNNs reduce energy by 90% while maintaining competitive accuracy on MNIST and CIFAR-10.
No single SNN paradigm dominates all performance axes; model selection depends on application constraints.

limitations: Evaluation relies primarily on benchmark datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, DVS128) that may not capture real-world deployment complexity. [unacknowledged]
Hardware-specific results are drawn from reported benchmarks in the literature rather than direct implementation. [unacknowledged]
Hyperparameter sensitivity in surrogate-gradient training and convergence instability in STDP remain challenges.
Scalability on high-dimensional tasks (e.g., ImageNet) and robustness under noisy conditions were not addressed.
